blindSummary:
Trans visitors face severe risk here — the most socially open country in its region layered over one of the region's most explicitly anti-trans statutes. One penal-code provision prescribes up to six years' imprisonment for "men disguising themselves as women" — a direct criminalisation of trans feminine expression. A second provision ("intercourse against the order of nature", up to 1 year) remains in force, though several courts have ruled it inapplicable to same-sex relations. Courts have granted legal gender recognition in some post-surgery cases since 1987, but inconsistently.

The capital's queer scene is the region's most visible — bars, LGBT-rights organisations and a documented court history — but the climate deteriorated sharply since 2022: state-affiliated militia groups attacked queer venues after an anti-discrimination bill was introduced, and a regional rights group documents rising prejudice and violence against trans people, particularly trans women, who face entrenched marginalisation and family and community violence.

For a visitor: the capital is navigable with discretion; visible trans feminine expression carries real (statutory) arrest risk; the economic collapse has degraded police predictability in both directions.
blindOutOfScope: Gender-recognition case law and healthcare pathologisation are for residents; the two penal-code statutes are traveller-facing.
blindSourceSummaries: Regional rights-group country review of this country: de facto and explicit criminalisation of trans expression (especially trans women) under penal-code provisions; rising prejudice and violence in the capital including attacks by state-affiliated militia groups on queer spaces after a decriminalisation bill was introduced; gradual progress on legal gender recognition since a 2015 judge's ruling emphasising the significance of transitioning; gender-affirming healthcare not prohibited and comparatively accessible, though privatised healthcare limits options.

Essay in a regional feminist publication (March 2022) on a confused judiciary and transgender rights: a survey of case law on legal gender recognition across several regional states including this country; no legislative framework, so trans people are forced into lengthy, costly judicial review where judges rely on outdated medical practices, selective religious-law readings and socio-religious bias, producing inconsistent rulings.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): the 'against the order of nature' provision is regularly used for arrests; several courts have ruled it does not apply to same-sex relations but it remains in force; trans people can change markers only after surgical procedures; in June 2022 the interior ministry banned gatherings 'promoting perversion'; a self-styled religious militia attacked queer bars and drag shows; LGBT organisations denounced the 2024 murder of a trans woman.

International human-rights organisation (May 2018): police shuttered pride events - security forces forced cancellation of pride events in the capital and detained organisers, using 'debauchery' charges and pressure on venues.

Foreign magazine (May 2018): profile of an activist who co-founded the first LGBT advocacy group in this country's region (2004) and was repeatedly dragged to capital police stations for interrogation and psychological pressure; now head of a regional LGBT foundation, campaigning across the wider region; recipient of a named international human-rights award.

International human-rights organisation (Feb 2017): this country edges closer to decriminalising same-sex conduct - a judge ruled that consensual same-sex conduct is not 'against nature', building on earlier rulings interpreting the provision narrowly.
